messages.author: e19ea506112fd25b
messages.subject: sample size predictive posterior
parts:
Hi,

Did anybody have experience on determining sample size in stan? Some authors use sample size predictive posterior as in "A Bayesian predictive sample size selection design for single-arm exploratory clinical trials." I also wonder how to incorporate prior information.

The problem is in pharma domain where production is in batches.  There are two variability components - between batch variability and within batch variability - which are not discussed in the paper.

Thanks for any insight,
Linas

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] sample size predictive posterior
parts:
Thanks, Bob. I wonder if there is a way to incorporate a prior knowledge?
Let's take cluster sampling example on pg. 448: investigators already
studied 300 persons from 10 U.S. Census tracts and got the estimate (in as
distribution not as single point) of interperson (within batch) and
intertract (between batches) variability. How to assess if those estimates
are good enough (i.e. are close to true variability) - maybe something
like 95% credible interval < X? How many more people/tracts we need to
sample to get better estimates (in case the 95% credible interval > X)?

Thank you,
Linas
On Wed, 07 Oct 2015 16:11:29 -0400, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> Andrew and Jennifer


--
Thank you,
Linas

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] sample size predictive posterior
parts:
I'm afraid I didn't understand the question. You can
always include prior knowledge in a Bayesian model. If you
have uncertainty in a parameter, integrate over it (usually
by sampling). As to calibrating vs. true uncertainty, you
can't just use simulation --- you need real data to assess things
like overdispersion of real data relative to a model.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] sample size predictive posterior
parts:
There’s no generic way of doing “sample size” calculations in
a Bayesian setting because the posterior concentration can
vary dramatically with the actual data measured. Considering
the worst case (for example minimum shrinkage) moves one
into the direction of Probabilistically Almost Correct (PAC)
methods that sort of have sample size equivalents. But really
if your posterior isn’t in the exponential family (in which case
you can do the usual methods) then there’s no “right” answer.
